translationRepairs: In the Taishi era he was named director of retainers for Jinxi, gentleman of the ministry of personnel's promotions section, and unimpeded-attendant gentleman.
In the Taishi era he was named director of retainers for Jinxi, gentleman of the ministry of works, and unimpeded-attendant gentleman.
尚書起部郎 names the Shangshu Board of Works (起部) gentleman; 'ministry of personnel's promotions section' invents the wrong bureau.
In the Taishi era he was appointed director of retainers for the Jinxi state, gentleman of the ministry of personnel's promotions section, and unimpeded-attendant gentleman.
In the Taishi era he was appointed director of retainers for the Jinxi state, gentleman of the ministry of works, and unimpeded-attendant gentleman.
Same office error in the literal: 起部 is Works, not personnel promotions.
In the second year of Jianyuan he issued an edict the court ministers: "The yellow register is the people's great charter and the state's hinge of order.
In the second year of Jianyuan he issued an edict to the court ministers: "The yellow register is the people's great charter and the state's hinge of order.
詔朝臣曰 requires a preposition before the addressees; 'issued an edict the court ministers' is ungrammatical English.
In the second year of Jianyuan he issued an edict the court ministers: "The yellow register is the people's great charter and the state's hinge of order.
In the second year of Jianyuan he issued an edict to the court ministers: "The yellow register is the people's great charter and the state's hinge of order.
Literal likewise lacks 'to' after 詔朝臣曰; inserting it restores grammatical English without changing sense.
Of forty-two brothers who shared the deepest mourning bond, through fortune and ruin, long life and early death, I alone remain.
Of forty-two brothers and cousins within the nine-month mourning degree, through fortune and ruin, long life and early death, I alone remain.
大功 is the nine-month mourning grade for collateral kin, not the deepest mourning bond. The revised wording explains the relationship without the inaccurate 'second-degree' label.
Without scheming for preferment I rose to the nine ministers; in virtue I am no Li Ling, yet I hold a post at the gate.
Without scheming for preferment I rose to the nine ministers; in virtue I am ashamed before Li Ling, yet I presumptuously hold a Menxia post.
德慙李陵 is shame before Li Ling, not denial of identity; 忝居門下 is a presumptuous Menxia post, not a generic gate post.

I passed through dark reigns and trampled chaos, forded hardship and walked on danger; I looked up to sage virtue to keep myself whole and leaned on worthy aides to hold my station. I never tired of bending before merit and power, never feared drowning among foxes and rats—yet the ground I stand on has not given way.

I passed through dark reigns and trampled chaos, forded hardship and walked on danger; I looked up to sage virtue to keep myself whole and leaned on worthy aides to hold my station. I never demeaned myself by yielding to merit and power, never feared drowning among foxes and rats—and the ground I stand on has not given way.
未嘗厭屈於勳權 means he never abased himself by yielding to the powerful; 'never tired of bending' reverses 厭屈.
Xiu first served as Commandant of the Horse Fleet, Court Attendant for Imperial Audiences, and regular attendant in Prince Xiangdong's establishment under Emperor Ming of Song.
Xiu first served as Commandant of Escort Cavalry, Court Attendant for Imperial Audiences, and regular attendant in the Xiangdong establishment of the future Emperor Ming of Song.
駙馬都尉 is the established Commandant of Escort Cavalry title, not a Horse Fleet command; 宋明帝湘東國 is the Xiangdong establishment of the future Emperor Ming.
Xiu first served as Commandant of the Horse Fleet, Court Attendant for Imperial Audiences, and regular attendant in Prince Xiangdong's establishment under Emperor Ming of Song.
Xiu first served as Commandant of Escort Cavalry, Court Attendant for Imperial Audiences, and regular attendant of the future Emperor Ming of Song's Xiangdong establishment.
駙馬都尉 is the established Commandant of Escort Cavalry title, and 宋明帝湘東國 identifies the future emperor's Xiangdong establishment.
Emperor Shun was the son of the Prince of Guiyang, Xiu Fan.
Emperor Shun was the son of the Prince of Guiyang, Xiufan.
休範 is one given name Xiufan; spacing it as Xiu Fan invents a false two-name form.
Yan Yuan answered without thinking, "As Your Majesty wills."
Yanyuan answered without thinking, "As Your Majesty wills."
彥遠 is the given name Yanyuan, matching 榮彥遠 in s0151; Yan Yuan is a false split.

When Shen Youzhi rose, Emperor Xiaowu took the joint army headquarters of the princes at Pencheng; Xiu handled military funds. After peace returned he became the Prince of Shaoling's pacification-of-the-south chief aide, then yellow gate officer, Ningshuo general, front-army chief aide, and Qi platform regular attendant.

When Shen Youzhi rose, Emperor Wu of Qi took the Jinxi and Shaoling princely headquarters and garrisoned Pencheng; Xiu handled military funds. After peace returned he became the Prince of Shaoling's pacification-of-the-south chief aide, then yellow gate officer, Ningshuo general, front-army chief aide, and Qi platform regular attendant.
In Nan Qi Shu, 世祖 is Emperor Wu of Qi; 挾晉熙邵陵二王軍府鎮盆城 names both princely headquarters and the Pencheng garrison. The temple-name gloss is unnecessary in idiomatic English.

During Shen Youzhi's rebellion, Emperor Xiaowu seized the military headquarters of the two princes at Pencheng; Xiu managed military expenses; when the matter was settled, he was moved to the Prince of Shaoling's Pacification of the South chief aide, made Yellow Gate Officer, Ningshuo general, front army chief aide, and Qi Platform Regular Attendant.

During Shen Youzhi's rebellion, Shizu, Emperor Wu of Qi, took the military headquarters of the Princes of Jinxi and Shaoling and garrisoned Pencheng; Xiu managed military expenses; when the matter was settled, he was moved to the Prince of Shaoling's Pacification of the South chief aide, made Yellow Gate Officer, Ningshuo general, front army chief aide, and Qi Platform Regular Attendant.
The literal field should retain 世祖 as Shizu while identifying Emperor Wu of Qi and restoring the omitted Jinxi and Shaoling headquarters.
As for my presumptuous excess, I should request bones and flesh."
As for my presumptuous excess, I should ask leave to resign and return home."
請骸骨 is the conventional resignation formula, not a request for bones and flesh; the idiomatic already has the right sense.
Under Yuankang, Yang Xin took up Zi Jing's standard clerical hand and the world bowed to it; the Right General's manner, a little old-fashioned, was no longer valued.
Under Yuanjia, Yang Xin took up Zi Jing's standard clerical hand and the world bowed to it; the Right General's manner, a little old-fashioned, was no longer valued.
元嘉 is the Liu Song Yuanjia reign, not Yuankang.
In the Yuankang era Yang Xin received Zi Jing's orthodox clerical method; the age together honored it; the Right General's style was slightly archaic and no longer prized.
In the Yuanjia era Yang Xin received Zi Jing's orthodox clerical method; the age together honored it; the Right General's style was slightly archaic and no longer prized.
Literal must likewise render 元嘉 as Yuanjia.
Under Yuankang he went out as secretary on the Prince of Jin'an's pacification of the west, came back as Situ chief clerk and magistrate of Shanyin, then became Situ recorder.
Under Yuanhui he went out as secretary on the Prince of Jin'an's pacification of the west, came back as Situ chief clerk and magistrate of Shanyin, then became Situ recorder.
元徽 is Yuanhui; Yuankang invents the wrong reign name.

In the Yuankang period he was sent out as Prince of Jin'an's Pacification of the West secretary, returned as Situ chief clerk and Magistrate of Shanyin, and transferred to Situ recorder staff officer.
In the Yuanhui period he was sent out as Prince of Jin'an's Pacification of the West secretary, returned as Situ chief clerk and Magistrate of Shanyin, and transferred to Situ recorder staff officer.
Literal shares the 元徽→Yuankang error; Yuanhui is required.
When the crown prince's son of Luling held Yingzhou, Chong served as his chief clerk, assisting-state general, and Jiangxia interior minister, running headquarters and provincial business.
When Champion General, Prince of Luling, Ziqing held Yingzhou, Chong served as his chief clerk, assisting-state general, and Jiangxia interior minister, running headquarters and provincial business.
冠軍廬陵王子卿爲郢州 is Champion General and Prince of Luling Ziqing assigned Yingzhou; 子卿 is not 'crown prince's son'.
The crown-prince's son of Luling, prince of Yingzhou, had Chong as chief clerk, assisting-state general, and Jiangxia interior minister, acting on headquarters and province affairs.
Champion General, Prince of Luling Ziqing, assigned to Yingzhou, had Chong as chief clerk, assisting-state general, and Jiangxia interior minister, acting on headquarters and province affairs.
The proposal rightly restores Ziqing and rejects 'prince of Yingzhou', but 'for Yingzhou' is awkward; 'assigned to Yingzhou' matches 爲郢州.

In Yongming, Yuan impeached Yuan Yi, grand administrator of Wu; in Jianwu, Yi's cousin's son Ang took the censor's seat and, within days, struck at Yuan's son Hui for letting his father travel in a hired white-canopy carriage—Hui was cashiered and barred from office.

In Yongming, Yuan impeached Yuan Tuan, grand administrator of Wuxing; in Jianwu, Tuan's younger cousin Ang took the censor's seat and, within days, struck at Yuan's son Hui for letting his father travel in a hired white-canopy carriage—Hui was cashiered and barred from office.
袁彖 is Yuan Tuan, 吳興 is Wuxing, and 從弟 is a younger cousin, not a cousin's son.

In Yongming Yuan impeached Yuan Yi, grand administrator of Wu commandery; in Jianwu Yi's cousin's son Ang became censor, and within days of taking office memorialized against Yuan's son Hui because his father rode in a rented white-canopy carriage—Hui was dismissed and forbidden from office.

In Yongming Yuan impeached Yuan Tuan, grand administrator of Wuxing commandery; in Jianwu Tuan's younger cousin Ang became censor, and within days of taking office memorialized against Yuan's son Hui because his father rode in a rented white-canopy carriage—Hui was dismissed and forbidden from office.
Literal needs the same three corrections: Yuan Tuan, Wuxing, and younger cousin.
The heir apparent had him receive the barbarian envoys, with added rank as attendant-in-ordinary.
The emperor ordered him to receive the barbarian envoys, with added rank as attendant-in-ordinary.
Here 世祖 is the reigning emperor (Emperor Wu of Qi); s0238–s0239 already call him 上/陛下, not the heir apparent.
The heir apparent ordered him to face the barbarian envoys, with added rank as attendant-in-ordinary.
The emperor ordered him to face the barbarian envoys, with added rank as attendant-in-ordinary.
Literal shares the heir-apparent misreading of 世祖; emperor is the right referent.
The emperor often sighed over the grace of his person; Wang Jian, seated beside him, said: "Set Gaozhi's cicada crown under the throne's radiance and his bearing only grows brighter.
The emperor often sighed over the grace of his person; Wang Jian, seated beside him, said: "Gaozhi looks all the more distinguished beneath the cicada crown.
杲之爲蟬冕所照 says the cicada crown enhances Gaozhi's appearance; the revised English preserves the image without a wooden passive construction.

He lived in poverty by choice; his table held only chive pickle, vinegared chives, raw chives, and humble greens. A wit said: "Who calls Minister Yu poor? When he dines on salmon he still has twenty-seven kinds."

He lived in poverty by choice; his table held only chive pickle, vinegared chives, raw chives, and humble greens. A wit said: "Who calls Minister Yu poor? When he dines on fish dishes he still has twenty-seven kinds."
鮭 in this three-chives joke is a general fish-dish term; salmon over-specifies a modern species.

Emperor Wu of Qi had known Chen in Emperor Ming of Song's reign and meant to use him well: aide to the state, chief staff officer to the Prince of Jin'an's southern center, grand administrator of Huainan, running headquarters and province.

Emperor Wu of Qi had known Chen in Emperor Ming of Song's reign and meant to entrust him with office. Chen became General Who Assists the State, chief clerk to the Prince of Jin'an as General of the Household for the South, and grand administrator of Huainan, with charge of both headquarters and provincial affairs.
輔國將軍 is a general's title, and 南中郎長史 is chief clerk to the prince in his capacity as General of the Household for the South. The revision states the offices in natural English.

The Shizu emperor had known Chen in Ming of Song's time and wished to entrust him; he was made aide to the state, chief staff officer to the Prince of Jin'an's southern center, and grand administrator of Huainan, acting for headquarters and province.

Shizu had known Chen in Emperor Ming of Song's time and wished to entrust him with office; Chen was made General Who Assists the State, chief clerk to the Prince of Jin'an as General of the Household for the South, and grand administrator of Huainan, acting for both headquarters and province.
The literal field retains 世祖 as Shizu while rendering 輔國將軍 and 南中郎長史 as actual offices rather than vague paraphrases.
To read old documents in vain only breeds the people's luck.
To leaf through old documents in vain only teaches the people to count on luck.
徒成民幸 means empty register-hunting only fosters the people's opportunistic reliance on luck, not breeding luck itself.
He held Vice Prefect of his home province.
He served as vice-prefect of his home province.
爲本州別駕 states that He Xian served in the provincial vice-prefect post; the old English is ungrammatical.
He held Vice Prefect of his home province.
He served as vice-prefect of his home province.
The idiomatic field shares the same ungrammatical office construction.
He was moved to Prince of Baling's chief clerk and made Secretariat Hall Attendant.
He was transferred to chief clerk to the Prince of Baling and appointed Palace Gentleman in the Department of State Affairs.
尚書殿中郎 is Palace Gentleman in the Department of State Affairs, not a generic secretariat hall attendant.
He became the Prince of Baling's chief clerk, then secretariat hall attendant.
He became chief clerk to the Prince of Baling, then Palace Gentleman in the Department of State Affairs.
The idiomatic field needs the same established office title.
When Emperor Xiaowu was in Jiangzhou, Chong was Pacification of the Distant Foe chief aide and Grand Administrator of Xunyang, and was greatly trusted.
When Shizu, the future Emperor Wu of Qi, governed Jiangzhou, Chong was chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs and Grand Administrator of Xunyang, and was greatly trusted.
In Nan Qi Shu, 世祖 is Xiao Ze, the future Emperor Wu of Qi, not Emperor Xiaowu of Liu Song; 征虜長史 is an office title.
While Emperor Xiaowu held Jiangzhou, Chong served as pacification-of-the-distant-foe chief aide and grand administrator of Xunyang, and was deeply trusted.
When the future Emperor Wu of Qi governed Jiangzhou, Chong served as chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs and grand administrator of Xunyang, and was deeply trusted.
The idiomatic field misidentifies 世祖 and obscures Chong's office.
When Xiaowu returned to the capital, he had Chong act for headquarters and province affairs.
When Shizu returned to the capital, he had Chong administer the headquarters and provincial affairs.
世祖 continues to refer to Shizu, not Emperor Xiaowu; 行府、州事 means administering headquarters and provincial affairs.
When Xiaowu came back to the capital he left Chong to run headquarters and provincial business.
When the future Emperor Wu returned to the capital, he left Chong in charge of headquarters and provincial affairs.
The idiomatic field repeats the wrong imperial identification.
When Emperor Xiaowu was in the Eastern Palace, he treated him as an old favor.
When Shizu was in the Eastern Palace, he treated Chong with the favor due an old retainer.
世祖 is Shizu and 恩舊 describes favor shown to a longstanding retainer, not treating someone 'as an old favor.'
While Xiaowu was still heir, he treated Chong as an old friend of the house.
While the future Emperor Wu was crown prince, he treated Chong with the favor due an old retainer.
The idiomatic field misidentifies the crown prince and weakens 恩舊.
Champion General, Prince of Luling Ziqing, assigned to Yingzhou, had Chong as chief clerk, assisting-state general, and Jiangxia interior minister, acting on headquarters and province affairs.

When Ziqing, Champion General and Prince of Luling, became Inspector of Yingzhou, he appointed Chong chief clerk, General Who Assists the State, and interior minister of Jiangxia, with charge of headquarters and provincial affairs.
爲郢州 denotes Ziqing's provincial appointment and 輔國將軍 is the title General Who Assists the State.
When Champion General, Prince of Luling, Ziqing held Yingzhou, Chong served as his chief clerk, assisting-state general, and Jiangxia interior minister, running headquarters and provincial business.

When Ziqing, Champion General and Prince of Luling, became Inspector of Yingzhou, Chong served as his chief clerk, General Who Assists the State, and interior minister of Jiangxia, with charge of headquarters and provincial affairs.
The earlier repair restored Ziqing but still omitted his inspectorship and left 輔國將軍 as a vague phrase.
Following the headquarters he became Anxi chief clerk and Nan commandery interior minister, acting on Jingzhou headquarters affairs; his generalship stood as before.

When the headquarters was transferred, Chong became chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West and interior minister of Nan Commandery, administering Jingzhou headquarters affairs; his general's title remained unchanged.
隨府轉 describes a transfer with the headquarters; 安西長史 is an office under the General Who Pacifies the West.
He followed the headquarters west, became Anxi chief clerk and Nan commandery interior minister, and ran Jingzhou headquarters affairs; his general's title was unchanged.

When the headquarters was transferred, Chong became chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West and interior minister of Nan Commandery, with charge of Jingzhou headquarters affairs; his general's title remained unchanged.
The old wording mistakes the title 安西 for a narrative movement west.

Yingzhou nominated him as xiucai; he was made outer military aide to the Prince of Jinxi's army-protector staff, merit recorder on the heir apparent's campaign-against-barbarians headquarters, and gentleman of the ministry chariot-and-horse bureau.

Yingzhou nominated him as xiucai; he was appointed outer military staff officer to the Prince of Jinxi as General Who Pacifies the West, merit officer in Shizu's headquarters as General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs, and Gentleman of the Chariot Bureau in the Department of State Affairs.
世祖 is Shizu, not a generic heir apparent, and the three offices require their full headquarters and bureau titles.

Yingzhou nominated him as xiucai; he became outer military aide on the Prince of Jinxi's army-protector staff, merit recorder on the heir apparent's pacification headquarters, and gentleman of the chariot-and-horse bureau.

Yingzhou nominated him as xiucai; he became outer military staff officer to the Prince of Jinxi as General Who Pacifies the West, merit officer in the future Emperor Wu of Qi's headquarters as General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs, and Gentleman of the Chariot Bureau in the Department of State Affairs.
The idiomatic field misidentifies 世祖 and compresses distinct official titles into misleading paraphrases.

He then became recorder on the heir apparent's pacification army and central army, was promoted to supernumerary regular cavalier attendant, then full attendant, was moved to secretariat gentleman, and held the rectifier posts for Jing and Xiang.

He then served as recorder in Shizu's headquarters as General of Pacification and General of the Central Army, was promoted to supernumerary Regular Mounted Attendant and then Regular Gentleman, moved to Secretariat Gentleman, and concurrently served as rectifier for Jingzhou and Xiangzhou.
世祖 is Shizu; 正員郎 is Regular Gentleman, and 領 marks the two rectifier posts as concurrent.

He became recorder on the heir apparent's pacification and central armies, rose to supernumerary regular cavalier attendant, then full attendant, was moved to secretariat gentleman, and held the rectifier posts for Jing and Xiang.

He then served as recorder in the future Emperor Wu of Qi's headquarters as General of Pacification and General of the Central Army, rose to supernumerary Regular Mounted Attendant and then Regular Gentleman, became Secretariat Gentleman, and concurrently served as rectifier for Jingzhou and Xiangzhou.
The old version misidentifies 世祖 and turns 正員郎 into a continuation of the preceding attendant title.
He was transferred to left vice director of the ministry of works; regular attendant and rectifier stood as before.
He was transferred to Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs; his Regular Mounted Attendant and rectifier posts remained as before.
尚書左丞 belongs to the Department of State Affairs, not the ministry of works.
He was made left vice director of the ministry of works while keeping his regular attendant and rectifier posts.
He became Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs while retaining his posts as Regular Mounted Attendant and rectifier.
The idiomatic field assigns 尚書左丞 to the wrong institution.

In Song's Daming era, when Shen Tanqing was in Xuzhou, Chen was summoned as reception chief clerk, then made reception staff officer for the province, constant attendant in the Prince of Xiangdong's kingdom, and northern campaign staff officer—all three lords, province, kingdom, and princely house, were Emperor Ming of Song.

In Song's Daming era, when Shen Tanqing was Inspector of Xuzhou, Chen was summoned as reception chief clerk, then made reception staff officer for the province, regular attendant in the Prince of Xiangdong's household, and northern-campaign staff officer; in the province, princely household, and headquarters alike, his lord was the future Emperor Ming of Song.
爲徐州 denotes Shen Tanqing's provincial appointment, while 州、國、府主皆宋明帝 says Chen served the future emperor through all three establishments.

Under Song's Daming reign Shen Tanqing held Xuzhou and called Chen in as reception chief clerk, then reception staff officer, constant attendant in the Prince of Xiangdong's household, and northern-campaign staff officer—province, kingdom, and princely seat alike belonged to Emperor Ming of Song.

Under Song's Daming reign, when Shen Tanqing was Inspector of Xuzhou, he summoned Chen as reception chief clerk. Chen later served as provincial reception officer, regular attendant in the Prince of Xiangdong's household, and northern-campaign staff officer; in all three posts his lord was the future Emperor Ming of Song.
The old English obscures both Tanqing's inspectorship and the repeated patron relationship expressed by 主.
He was moved to Yellow Gate, then regular attendant, aide to the state, staff officer to the Prince of Jiangxia's right army, and champion general.
He was transferred to Yellow Gate Gentleman, then Regular Mounted Attendant, General Who Assists the State, chief clerk to the Prince of Jiangxia's Right Army, and Champion General.
輔國將軍 and 右軍長史 are formal titles, not generic descriptions.
He became yellow gate officer, then regular attendant, aide to the state, staff officer on the Prince of Jiangxia's right army, and champion general.
He became Yellow Gate Gentleman, then Regular Mounted Attendant, General Who Assists the State, chief clerk to the Prince of Jiangxia's Right Army, and Champion General.
The idiomatic field needs the same formal office titles.

The Prince of Xiyang, Ziming, was in Southern Yanzhou; when chief staff officer Shen Xian left office, the emperor moved Chen again to chief staff officer on the Pacify-the-Barbarians command, acting for the southern Yan headquarters and province; his generalship stood as before.

When Ziming, Prince of Xiyang, was Inspector of Southern Yanzhou and chief clerk Shen Xian left office, the emperor transferred Chen there as chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs, with charge of Southern Yanzhou headquarters and provincial affairs; his general's title remained unchanged.
在南兖州 states Ziming's provincial posting, and 征虜長史 is chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs.

The Prince of Xiyang, Ziming, held Southern Yanzhou; when chief staff officer Shen Xian quit, the emperor set Chen again as pacify-the-barbarians chief staff officer, acting for headquarters and province, generalship unchanged.

When Ziming, Prince of Xiyang, was Inspector of Southern Yanzhou and his chief clerk Shen Xian left office, the emperor transferred Chen there as chief clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs, with charge of headquarters and provincial affairs; his general's title remained unchanged.
The old version implies possession of the province and mistranslates the office title.

東海 is a place-name component
Ancheng is a place-name component of the princely title
神州 is a geographic epithet
Xiang region place-name in 南湘
